title: Prophecy and discernment
hookLine: a word for someone, tested by scripture and the church (1 Corinthians 14:29)

cards: What should a church do when someone stands up and says God has given them a word? In the meetings Paul writes to, one person has a psalm, another a teaching, another a word they say came from God.
He doesn't tell them to stop. He gives them an order: "Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge." Speak, then weigh.

In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, that pairing is still alive. Someone may stand during worship and say they sense a word for the room, or quietly tell one person something they believe God put on their heart.
Then the church listens, and tests it.

teach.b: In Paul's letter, prophecy isn't fortune-telling. He says what it's for in the same chapter: "he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort."
Edification means building up; in the same letter Paul tells the church, "ye are God's building." Build up, urge on, comfort: three jobs.
By Paul's measure, a word that only tears someone down has missed its job before anyone checks it. Then comes the weighing.
Paul tells another church: "Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Don't sneer at it, and don't swallow it whole.
John's first letter says it more sharply: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God."

In charismatic churches, a word is weighed against scripture by leaders and by the congregation, and the person who gave it is expected to take it humbly if it's set aside. A word doesn't outrank the Bible or the body.
Christians read this gift in different ways. Pentecostals and charismatics hold that the gift is still given today, as in the New Testament.
Some other Protestants hold that prophecy as new revelation ended with the apostles, and hear Paul's words as being about preaching and teaching scripture.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of prophetic gifts in the church, tested by the church's teaching.
And Paul's test works on any sentence spoken over someone, at work, at the dinner table, in a text at midnight: does it build up?

how: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, someone may share a word they believe is from God, during worship or privately, and pastors and the congregation weigh it against scripture before anyone acts on it.

games.q: during worship someone stands and says God has given them a word. by Paul's instruction, what should the church do?
o: accept it at once, since it's from God.
let them speak, then weigh what was said.
silence them, since prophecy causes trouble.
games.why: Paul does both: let the prophets speak, and let the others judge. the word is welcomed and tested.

practice: Bring one person to mind who could use building up this week, and let a kind word come slowly: not flattery or advice, but something true about them that would hold weight, like a beam in a house.
Then test it Paul's way: does it build up, urge on, or comfort? If you pray, hold that person before God while you choose; if you don't, simply hold them with care.

wordCard.voice: Prophecy and discernment. A word spoken to build others up, and the church's work of weighing it against scripture.

orig.note: Greek: a building, and the act of building up. Paul's word for what prophecy is for in 1 Corinthians 14:3.

carryVoice: Your line: build up. Speak first, then weigh it with care. That's today, done.
